raw_case_text:
A 51-year-old woman with a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and dysfunctional uterine bleeding presented with progressive lower extremity swelling of 3 weeks duration. The swelling was associated with pain and tenderness when palpated, without warmth or erythema. She reported having regular heavy menses for 5 years, that stopped after menopause 2 years prior. She denied exertional chest pain, shortness of breath, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, cough, fever, weight loss, or dysuria. The patient denied any history of intravenous drug use. On physical examination, she was afebrile, with jugular vein distention and +3 bilateral lower limb edema. Lungs were clear and cardiac sounds had regular rate and rhythm. A grade III/VI holosystolic murmur was heard on the left lower sternal border. The abdomen was distended, but soft, with mild tenderness on suprapubic area with active bowel sounds. No skin rash, Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, or splinter hemorrhages were noticed on examination. No stigmata of chronic liver disease were seen. Initial labs revealed mild thrombocytopenia with normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein. Electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm and incomplete right bundle branch block. Transthoracic echocardiogram showed severe tricuspid regurgitation and tricuspid valve vegetation with normal ejection fraction (Figure 1 and Supplemental Video 1). Computed tomography (CT) pulmonary angiogram showed a filling defect in the left lower pulmonary artery suspicious for calcified embolus and multiple bilateral sub-centimeter pulmonary nodules in the lower lungs that appeared to be contiguous with the vasculature. A transesophageal echocardiogram showed a large vegetation oscillating between the right ventricle and right atrium on the posterior and septal leaflets of the tricuspid valve, and small vegetations on the anterior leaflet.
Infectious workup, including multiple blood cultures, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, Chlamydophila psittaci, Brucella, Bartonella, Coxiella burnetii antibodies, and Legionella antigen were all negative. All autoimmune workup was negative.
Potential causes for tricuspid valve vegetation include infectious, aseptic from autoimmune disease, or, rarely, malignancy. Computed tomography pulmonary angiogram appeared to be consistent with septic emboli; however, given the lack of infectious and autoimmune source, metastasis was suspected.
Abdominal imaging including CT and magnetic resonance imaging showed a large fundal fibroid with cystic degeneration and an exophytic fibroid extending toward the left adnexa. Endometrial biopsy showed endometrial and endocervical tissue with tubal metaplasia without atypia or malignancy.
Due to severe symptomatic primary tricuspid regurgitation due to aseptic vegetation, the patient underwent cardiothoracic surgery. Intraoperatively, a discrete mass attached to the tricuspid valve tissue was found, measuring 2.37 cm x 1.15 cm. Severe degeneration and destruction of all valve leaflets was noticed, sub-valvular abscess was debrided, and the valve was replaced with #31 Epic St Jude tissue valve. The patient tolerated the surgery well without any complications. During her follow-up in the cardiology clinic, her symptoms of shortness of breath and lower limb swelling showed a significant improvement.
Microscopically (Figure 2), it was smooth muscle neoplasm without significant nuclear atypia and no identifiable mitosis or necrosis. Diffuse and strong positivity for desmin and smooth muscle antibodies were positive. In addition, there was diffuse positivity for estrogen, progesterone, and Wilms tumor gene 1, suggesting likely uterine origin, and represented BML. Post-operatively, total hysterectomy is planned, with risk/benefits discussion of hormonal blocking agents to follow.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 51-year-old woman presented with a 3-week history of progressive, painful bilateral lower extremity swelling.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 51-year-old woman developed progressive bilateral lower limb swelling over 3 weeks, associated with pain and tenderness on palpation but without warmth or erythema.
subjective.past_medical_history: Hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and history of dysfunctional uterine bleeding (heavy regular menses for 5 years prior to menopause 2 years ago). Denied history of intravenous drug use.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for painful lower extremity swelling; negative for exertional chest pain, shortness of breath, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, cough, fever, weight loss, or dysuria.

objective.physical_examination: Afebrile; jugular venous distention and +3 bilateral lower extremity pitting edema. Lungs clear to auscultation; regular cardiac rate and rhythm with a grade III/VI holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border. Abdomen distended but soft with mild suprapubic tenderness and active bowel sounds. No skin rash, Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, splinter hemorrhages, or stigmata of chronic liver disease.
objective.routine_investigations: Mild thrombocytopenia with normal ESR and CRP. ECG showed sinus rhythm with incomplete right bundle branch block. Transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) revealed severe tricuspid regurgitation and a tricuspid valve vegetation with normal ejection fraction.
objective.advanced_workup: CT pulmonary angiogram showed a filling defect in the left lower pulmonary artery suspicious for calcified embolus and multiple bilateral sub-centimeter lower lobe pulmonary nodules contiguous with the vasculature. Transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) demonstrated a large oscillating vegetation between the right ventricle and right atrium on the posterior and septal tricuspid leaflets plus small vegetations on the anterior leaflet. Autoimmune workup negative. Abdominal CT and MRI showed a large fundal fibroid with cystic degeneration and an exophytic fibroid extending toward the left adnexa. Endometrial biopsy showed benign endometrial/endocervical tissue with tubal metaplasia. Intraoperative exploration revealed a 2.37 cm x 1.15 cm discrete mass on the tricuspid valve with severe leaflet destruction; histopathology and immunohistochemistry demonstrated a benign smooth muscle neoplasm (desmin+, SMA+, ER+, PR+, WT1+) without atypia, mitosis, or necrosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Infective endocarditis was ruled out with negative multiple blood cultures and negative serologies/antigens for Brucella, Bartonella, Coxiella burnetii, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, Chlamydophila psittaci, and Legionella. Histopathology and immunohistochemistry of the resected tricuspid valve mass confirmed benign metastasizing leiomyoma (BML) of uterine origin masquerading as tricuspid valve endocarditis. The patient underwent surgical debridement and tricuspid valve replacement with a #31 Epic St. Jude bioprosthetic valve, resulting in marked improvement of dyspnea and lower limb edema on cardiology follow-up, with total hysterectomy and hormonal blockade planned.
